failure: After lifting patternToRegex and specificity to pi-extension-utils, the runner's permissions.test.ts kept 13 tests duplicating the lifted tests.

failure: Agent treated .pi/extensions/pi-permission-system/config.json as personal/unstaged and avoided committing it.
correction: Project-level config files under .pi/ are project settings, not personal — stage and commit them as part of the work.

failure: Passed `run` tool's `cmd` as `["pnpm install"]` — one element containing the whole string. Runner joins argv with spaces, so it became the binary name "pnpm install" → ENOENT.
correction: `cmd` is `string[]` of argv tokens, not a single string. Split at every space: `["pnpm", "install"]`, never `["pnpm install"]`. Verify by checking if the first element contains a space.
context: First session exploration of run-tool argv semantics. 6-8 turns of "command not found" before the user stepped in. The runner's allowlist was matching; the argv form was wrong.

failure: After being told cmd is an array, kept retrying the same single-string-in-array form and getting the same error. Did not verify the form had actually changed.
correction: When retrying a failing call, compare new argv literally to the previous. If identical, the mistake is unchanged — do not retry the same form.
context: Four rounds of "no you're not" / "you're still treating the run command like bash" before the user pointed at the right command. ~3-4 turns of failed pnpm retries.

failure: When `run` returned "command not found", interpreted it as pnpm missing from PATH, not as argv-form misuse. Jumped to environment-debugging instead of checking the first element.
correction: `run`'s "command not found" with an allowlisted command is argv-form misuse. Distinguish by looking at the first element of `cmd` — if it contains a space, the form is wrong.
context: pnpm was genuinely not in PATH, but the surface signal ("command not found") was identical to the argv-form error. ~3 turns of environment debugging before the user fixed the form.

failure: Shipped STOCK_CONFIG with pre-baked opinions — `*.env: deny`, `pnpm run *: allow`, verdicts for every extension tool. User wanted only the fail-closed default and 7 built-in tools.
correction: A fail-closed system's stock config contains ONLY the fail-closed default and hardcoded surfaces. The user owns the policy decisions; the system never pre-blocks, never pre-allows.
context: User: "do not auto block any paths, also no pre filters for bash". Override semantic is correct, but shipping opinionated was the wrong default. ~3 turns to rewrite STOCK_CONFIG.

failure: Added 4 tests that asserted hardcoded STOCK_CONFIG values like `expect(config.aspects).toEqual({})`. The test re-asserts the literal — if the literal changes, the test breaks, but it exercises no logic.
correction: Tests assert behavior, not data. A test that compares an object to a hardcoded literal of itself is documentation, not verification. Loader/merger tests should exercise the loader/merger.
context: User: \"there is little value in testing that a hardcoded object has certain values\". Had to delete 4 data-shape tests and rewrite the file. The malformed-JSON test stayed. ~3 turns.

failure: Misread the eslint column as the failing token's start — it is the byte offset of the offending char. Cycled through guessing which `?.` was unnecessary by re-reading the file.
correction: When given an eslint file:line:col error, count chars from col 1. The line content already in the conversation is authoritative — don't re-read.
context: 3 rounds guessing which `?.` was unnecessary before using read to dump the line. The column already said everything. ~2 turns wasted.

failure: Fine-grained edits left duplicate or truncated lines — edit's oldText matched a substring but the new text was for larger context. Edit reported success but the file was wrong.
correction: After every edit, read the affected region (5-10 lines) to verify literal state. Edit only checks oldText was found, not that the result is correct.
context: Two incidents: duplicate line, truncated line. Both required follow-up read+edit. ~2 turns wasted.
